absent: Locking and concurrency rules for vCPU flags, CPU context registers, VNCR backing, host per-CPU data, VM identification registers, and fine-grained trap state.
Memory ordering and barrier requirements beyond the single barrier noted for direct hypervisor calls.
Full layouts of CPU context, vCPU arch state, VM arch state, and generic stat structures referenced but not defined here.
Definitions and numeric encodings of system register identifiers, trap group identifiers, and feature field limits referenced by name.
Error handling and recovery for secure monitor call failures beyond warning and substitution noted.
Lifecycle and ownership transitions for floating-point and debug register states and for unsupported-CPU marking.
Trace buffer descriptor layout and hypervisor trace lifecycle.

findings.text: Per-vCPU state word reserves consecutive positions for KVM state: host single-step active pending at 3, guest single-step active pending at 4, PMUSERENR on CPU at 5, wait-for-interrupt at 6, nested return at 7, nested SError pending at 8, nested exception at 9.

A vCPU derives its vector quadword count from its configured maximum vector length, selects the EL2 control register when in hypervisor context and the EL1 variant otherwise, and computes its vector state footprint from that length with zero returned when the length is invalid. Guest vector availability requires both system-wide support and a per-VM guest flag.
Valid guest debug control is the combination of enable, software breakpoint, hardware assist, and single-step request bits; no other control bit is accepted.

Vector presence for a vCPU is evaluated through a hypervisor-address translation of its VM in one build and directly from its VM in the other. Pointer authentication presence either requires a final address or generic capability together with a matching per-vCPU address or generic feature, or is unconditionally absent in the alternate build.
Whether a vCPU sits on an unsupported physical CPU is recorded as a single flag with separate query, set, and clear operations.

System register storage for a CPU context normally uses the context register array, but when nested virtualization is finalized and the index lies in the VNCR window with a backing array present the VNCR backing entry is used instead. A wrapper adds a compile-time range check against the register count for constant indices.

Assigning or read-modify-writing a vCPU system register applies per-register sanitisation masks whenever nested virtualization is active for that vCPU and the index reaches the sanitised range, then stores the result in the context.

VM statistics wrap only generic VM counters. VCPU statistics wrap generic VCPU counters plus dedicated 64-bit counters for HVC exits, WFE exits, WFI exits, user-space MMIO exits, kernel MMIO exits, signal exits, and total exits.

Hypervisor invocation has enhanced and non-enhanced forms. In one build the void form calls directly with a barrier on enhanced hosts and routes through a secure monitor call otherwise, while the returning form captures the callee result on enhanced hosts and the monitor result otherwise; the monitor path warns when status is not success and substitutes a not-supported error payload. In the alternate build all forms collapse to direct calls.

A performance interrupt is considered in-guest only when guest performance events are compiled in and the vCPU pointer is non-null. A PMU counter is treated as deferred only on non-enhanced hosts when its attribute requests host exclusion.
Paravirtual steal-time starts with its base set to an invalid guest address; it is reported enabled exactly when the base differs from that sentinel.

Per-CPU host data is addressed directly in one build and selected by a protected-mode static branch between normal and hypervisor-symbol access in the other. A flags word in that area supports test, set, and clear of individually named host-data flags.

Floating-point register ownership is a per-CPU state read from host data with distinct guest-owned and host-owned values. Debug register ownership is a per-vCPU tri-state of free, host-owned, or guest-owned with predicates for any use and for each owner. The OS lock is reported enabled when the lock bit in the OS lock status register is set.

Host CPU context initialization records the immutable host MPIDR into the MPIDR register slot. Idmapped vectors are required only when the Spectre V3A mitigation capability is finalized. IRQ bypass is unconditionally available, and hypervisor reservation is a no-op.

In this configuration PMU event set and clear, TRBE enable and disable, and EL1 tracing configuration accept their arguments and do nothing, while setting the user-mode PMU enable register always reports failure.
The build advertises architecture-specific VM allocation and two forms of remote TLB invalidation as available.

A VM is protected only when protected KVM is globally enabled and its per-arch protected flag is set; a vCPU inherits that status from its VM. Memory tagging availability needs system support plus a per-VM enable flag. 32-bit EL0 support needs system support and absence of a mismatched EL0 static branch. Run-once, vector-finalized, and initialized states are single-bit flags, and vCPU features are tested as bits in the arch feature bitmap.

VM identification register storage maps a contiguous system-register range to indexed entries in an ID array, routes four architected identification registers to dedicated fields, and otherwise warns once and yields a null pointer. Reading a VM identification register dereferences that storage.
System register identifiers encode five fields into one value using per-field shifts, and decoders recover each field with shift and mask operations.

Feature fields are extracted from VM identification registers as unsigned values, optionally sign-extended using per-field width and signedness metadata, with enum reads treated as unsigned. Comparison helpers evaluate signed, unsigned, or automatically selected signedness against a named limit, equality for enums, and inclusive ranges via paired comparisons.

Pointer authentication is present only when exactly one of three algorithm families meets its minimum level while its generic counterpart meets the implemented level. Stage-1 PIE and RAS presence follow their feature fields, while stage-1 POE additionally requires system-wide POE support.

Fine-grained trap registers are grouped so that read and write variants of the same control share a group, with separate groups for second-generation controls and for interrupt-controller traps. Access selects the write bank for write-trap registers and the read bank otherwise.
Hypervisor, hypervisor-event, hypertrace, MMU, MTE, and nested header guards each define a unique inclusion sentinel. A hypervisor byteswap helper provides 32-bit constant swapping.

Exception-level system-register access has a fixed-mapping build that redirects EL0, EL1, and EL2 names to their virtualized aliases, and a patchable build that selects between native and virtualized encodings at boot based on a VHE capability key, which itself resolves to one of two capability constants depending on configuration.
Hypervisor entry and exit are classified into SMC, HVC, system, PSCI, host abort, guest exit, host return, guest return, and an unknown value that must remain last.
Hypertrace description holds a backing region start and size plus an embedded trace-buffer descriptor. Event identity pairs a numeric identifier with an atomic enable flag.

Nested translation converts an EL2 translation control into an EL1 form by disabling the upper address range, mapping shareability and tag-inclusion bits, translating the physical size into the intermediate size field, and preserving granule and memory-type fields. Control conversion keeps only a minimal supported bit set and forces reserved-one bits, while base conversion clears the address-space identifier.
Stage-2 translation result records output physical address, block size, writability, readability, lookup level, syndrome, and raw descriptor, each exposed through a dedicated accessor.

Execute permission for EL0 and EL1 is decoded from two execute-never bits, collapsed to a single effective bit when extended execute-never support is absent. EL0 allows the two encodings that permit user execution, EL1 allows the two that permit privileged execution, and extended support itself needs both a CPU capability and a VM feature.

Support for stage-1 TLB invalidation at EL1 and EL2 requires matching operation fields, an accepted shareability encoding with the extra-speculation form gated on an XS feature, an outer-shareable form gated on an OS feature, and range forms gated on a RANGE feature. The EL2 form additionally rejects two intermediate-physical-address variants.
Authenticated return emulation is unreachable and always fails after recording a fault sentinel for the return address.
Unknown identification registers yield a null storage pointer after a one-time warning, and invalid vector lengths yield a zero state size, so callers must handle empty results.
External field extraction relied upon for register and descriptor decoding.
External one-time warning relied upon for invalid-state reporting.
Alternate build of one-time warning relied upon for invalid-state reporting.
Second alternate build of one-time warning relied upon for invalid-state reporting.
External bit test relied upon for feature and state flags.
External mask construction relied upon for address field clearing.
Alternate build of mask construction relied upon for address field clearing.
External compile-time check relied upon for register range and trap-group validation.
External configuration test relied upon for optional guest feature handling.
